courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Memory cost, ablations, failure modes and gsplat in practice
md: 3DGS trades memory for speed: hundreds of megabytes of explicit parameters instead of a few megabytes of network weights, in exchange for rendering at well over 30 FPS and training in tens of minutes.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
md: Removing a stage is not always a clean subtraction. You must decide what replaces it: no rewrite at all, or a trivial rewrite; BM25 alone, or BM25 with more candidates to keep the reranker's input size equal. State the replacement, because different choices give different deltas.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: IDOR and BOLA: changing one number in the URL
md: The OWASP API Security Top 10 warns that comparing the session's user id with an id parameter covers only a small subset of BOLA cases. Objects are often shared (a team folder, a manager viewing a report), so the real question is "may this user perform this action on this object under our policy", which lessons 11 and 12 turn into one reusable check.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Enforce authorization in one place: deny by default, policy engines
md: Central does not mean single. Next.js apps that checked access only in middleware were exposed when CVE-2025-29927 let requests skip middleware (lesson 7). Decide policy in one place, but enforce it at more than one layer: at the route, and again at the data (scoped queries, RLS).

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Kerberoasting: service tickets that can be cracked offline
md: Moving a service account to AES is not a fix by itself. An AES ticket for `Summer2019!` is still crackable; it only costs more per guess. The fix is a password nobody can guess: a gMSA or a long random secret.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AD CS: when a certificate template hands out admin
md: In AD a certificate trusted for client authentication is a password that survives password resets. ESC1 is a template that lets any user choose the name in the certificate. Audit templates, treat CAs as Tier 0, watch 4886 and 4887 for mismatched subjects, and revoke rather than reset.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Return-oriented programming as Shacham defined it
md: Misconception: "ROP needs special gadget functions, so removing dangerous library functions stops it." Shacham's thesis is the opposite: any large enough body of x86 code contains enough sequences, many of them unintended. The fix is checking control flow, not pruning code.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Command and control at the design level
md: Do not treat C2 detection as "find the red team's tool". CISA's federal red team (AA24-193A) "deployed over seven different implants" with different host and network signatures precisely to show that defenders who hunt one framework's fingerprints miss the rest. Detect the behaviour every implant shares: periodic contact, new destinations, odd egress from servers.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Reporting, retesting and where to practise
md: Measure a red or purple team by what it changes: findings with owners, fixes retested with the same procedure, and tests that keep running afterwards. Everything is done under written authorisation, inside agreed rules, with a way to stop in minutes.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: From one model call to an agent loop
md: The model does not execute tools. It only emits a structured request. Whether a shell command actually runs, and with what permissions, is decided entirely by harness code, which is why safety controls belong in the harness.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The read path: scoring memories by recency, importance and relevance
md: Recency decay does not resolve conflicts. A stale fact with high importance and relevance still makes the cut, so the newer fact helps only if the reader happens to trust it more. Resolve contradictions on the write path; use scoring to choose among facts that are all still true.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: From a benchmark to an environment: reset, step and a checker
md: An agentic RL environment is a benchmark task turned into a loop you can run millions of times: `reset` to a clean sandbox, `step` per tool call, and a programmatic checker that produces the reward at the end. The simulated user in tau-bench is part of the environment, not part of the policy.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: A toy agent loop: watching a web page give orders
md: The dangerous line is never the model call. It is the loop that turns model output into actions. Put your controls there.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Model supply chain: pickle files, safetensors and signing
md: Loading a pickle is running code. Prefer safetensors, load PyTorch files with weights_only=True, and verify a signature or hash from a source you trust before loading anything.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Cheap surrogates for DFT: graph networks and interatomic potentials
md: Judge a discovery surrogate by what it does to DFT spending: precision (hit rate), recall, and DAF on unrelaxed inputs. A low regression error does not guarantee good decisions near the hull.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Distortion-free sampling: the Gumbel trick and SynthID tournaments
md: Green lists shift probabilities toward a keyed subset (distortionary). Gumbel sampling and two-competitor tournaments keep each token's distribution exact and hide the signal in correlations between chosen tokens and keyed random values. All of them need entropy to work.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Isolation Forest: anomalies split off in fewer random cuts
md: The fixed 0.5 cutoff of contamination="auto" is not calibrated to your data. In the 1000-point evaluation set of lesson 5 it flags 241 points when only 10 are anomalies. Rank by score, or set the threshold from a review budget, rather than trusting the default label.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: APIs from zero: REST, GraphQL and what a request carries
md: Misconception: "Only our app calls this API, so it is private." The app's traffic can be read and replayed by anyone who installs it, and API keys built into an app can be extracted from it. Treat every request as if a stranger typed it by hand.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Redirect URIs, the state parameter and OAuth CSRF
md: Misconception: state is optional decoration. Without state, PKCE, or nonce, any OAuth client can be logged into an attacker's account. RFC 6749 and RFC 9700 both make CSRF protection a must.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Case: Storm-0558 and the forged Microsoft tokens (2023)
md: A valid signature is only as good as the question "is this key one that this issuer uses for this kind of token?" RFC 8725 says it plainly: check that the keys belong to the issuer. And signing keys are crown jewels: rotate them, retire them, alert on their age, and log every use.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Secure code review: what a reviewer looks for
md: Review the flows, not the lines. For every value from outside, follow it to each sink and check the control at each trust boundary. Then ask the questions a tool cannot: should this exist, and who may use it?

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: CVE assignment and CNAs: who names a vulnerability
md: Fewer CVEs is not the same as fewer vulnerabilities. A vendor that fixes bugs silently looks clean while customers' scanners have nothing to match and never flag the old version. Judge vendors by how fast and how well they publish, not by the count.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: LSNs, pageLSN and the two tables recovery rebuilds
md: Do not mix up pageLSN and recLSN. In the example, P1 was first dirtied at LSN 10 and last changed at 60, so its recLSN is 10 while its pageLSN is 60. recLSN says where redo for the page might need to start; pageLSN says which changes the page already contains.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: A toy run: how the input type flips the top result
md: Simplified: real embeddings are not interpretable feature lists, and the size of the effect varies by model and corpus. The toy shows the direction of the failure, not its typical magnitude. Lesson 5 is about measuring the magnitude on your data.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Why waiting on threads is expensive and coroutines are cheap
md: Async does not make one request faster. It makes **waiting cheap**: a waiting connection costs a small saved object instead of a blocked OS thread with its own stack, so a few threads can serve many thousands of mostly idle connections.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Compare-and-swap: write only if nothing changed, else retry
md: CAS compares values, not history. If the value goes from A to B and back to A between your load and your CAS, the CAS succeeds as if nothing happened. For a counter that is harmless. For pointers in lock-free data structures (structures built from atomics instead of locks) it can be a real bug, the **ABA problem**, which has its own course later.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Who are you, prove it, and what may you do?
md: Identification is a claim, authentication is proof of the claim, authorization is permission. MFA means two different *kinds* of factor, not two secrets of the same kind.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: After login: session tokens, fixation, expiry and logout
md: A session token is a password with an expiry date. Make it random (64+ bits), send it only as a Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookie, replace it at login, expire it on the server, and destroy it on the server at logout.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Orchestrator, parallel subagents and context isolation
md: More subagents is not automatically better. Anthropic's early agents spawned 50 subagents for simple queries and distracted each other with updates. Their prompts now embed effort rules: simple fact-finding gets 1 agent with 3 to 10 tool calls, direct comparisons get 2 to 4 subagents with 10 to 15 calls each, and complex research uses more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: On-demand capacity: tokens per minute and the max_tokens trap
md: Specific burndown rates, default quotas and tier prices change as models launch. Treat any number you remember as stale and read the current quota page and model card before you size a workload.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers
md: Loading the 2B4T checkpoint in Hugging Face `transformers` (the standard Python model library) saves memory but gives no speed or energy gain; the model card says the efficiency needs the dedicated bitnet.cpp kernels.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: B+trees update in place, and random writes pay for it
md: A B+tree's write cost is set by the **page**, not the row: a random small update rewrites a whole page at a random location. Reads are cheap because each key lives in exactly one place.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: The buffer pool: frames, a page table, pins and dirty pages
md: A buffer pool is a write-back page cache owned by the database. On a miss it must evict some *unpinned* page, and write it out first if it is *dirty*. Everything else in this course is about choosing that page well.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Business impact analysis: from processes to tolerable downtime
md: A BIA turns "everything is critical" into an ordered list: for each process, the impact over time, the resources it needs, and its maximum tolerable downtime, decided by the people who own the loss. Everything later (targets, backups, sites, tests) is sized from it.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Restoring at the right size: Atlassian's two-week outage, April 2022
md: Prevent mass deletion at the API (typed IDs, previews, batch caps, second approvers), make deletion reversible for a period (soft delete), and practise restores at the sizes you will really need. Atlassian met its RPO and still took up to 14 days, because its restore procedure did not fit the shape of the loss.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Crisis management: decisions, workarounds and communication
md: Crisis management decides and speaks; recovery teams fix. Keep a decision log, a fixed update rhythm, one authorised voice, contact lists stored outside production, and manual workarounds written down before they are needed.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Entropy patching: spend compute where the next byte is hard
md: Entropy patching spends a global step where the next byte is hard to predict and lets cheap local layers handle predictable runs. The threshold sets the average patch size, and therefore the compute.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Why C memory bugs compile cleanly and ship
md: C's type system cannot express *who owns this block* or *how long this pointer is valid*. Rust's ownership and borrow rules are exactly that missing information, checked at compile time.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Build a safe type on unsafe: a minimal Vec from scratch
md: MyVec is a teaching subset. It rejects zero-sized types, has no insert, remove, iterators or slice access, and does not handle a panic in the middle of an operation. The Rustonomicon's later Vec chapters add each of these, which is a measure of how much care std's Vec holds.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: The working-set staircase and average access time
md: Think in **miss rate**, not hit rate. CMU's point: 99% hits is twice as fast as 97% when misses cost 100 cycles, because the misses dominate the time.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Why raw clicks teach a ranker to repeat itself
md: A low CTR at rank 4 does not mean a document is less relevant than one at rank 1. CTR mixes two things: how often the slot is seen and how good the document is. You must separate them before clicks can serve as relevance labels.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Stored XSS and the worms it made: Samy and TweetDeck
md: Both worms are stored XSS that spread because the payload could use the victim's session to store itself again. Both trace back to a gap in **output encoding**: a filter that guessed at browser parsing (MySpace) and one rendering path that skipped escaping (TweetDeck). Encoding has to happen on every path, as the very last step before data enters HTML.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Why CLIP learns from captions instead of fixed labels
md: CLIP does not learn to describe images. It learns two encoders whose outputs agree: a matching image and caption land close together in one shared vector space, and non-matching ones land apart. Everything else in this course (zero-shot classification, retrieval, the failure modes) follows from that geometry.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Blind spots: data events, flow logs and traffic you never see
md: Misconception: "VPC Flow Logs record every packet on the network". They record summaries per flow, aggregated over up to 10 minutes by default (1 minute on Nitro instances), and they skip whole categories of traffic, including the instance metadata service and Amazon DNS.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Snowflake 2024 and SaaS platforms: hunting from the customer's side
md: Misconception: "the vendor was not breached, so this is the vendor's problem". In both Snowflake 2024 and Salesloft Drift 2025, the evidence, the containment levers (users, network policies, tokens, secrets) and the exposure decision sat with each customer.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Serverless: execution roles, event injection and function secrets
md: Serverless removes servers, not responsibility. A function is code plus a role plus its triggers: validate every event as untrusted input, give each function only the role it needs, and keep secrets in a secret store rather than in configuration.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: How AWS decides: explicit deny, SCPs, boundaries and resource policies
md: "We added an Allow, so it should work" is the classic debugging trap. If anything anywhere has a matching `Deny`, including an SCP you cannot see from inside the account, no Allow will help. AWS's documentation advises asking your organization's administrators when an SCP might be the cause.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Incident response for a leaked cloud key
md: For a leaked key: deactivate first, then investigate with CloudTrail across all Regions, then hunt for persistence (new users, keys, roles and policies) before declaring it closed. Then remove the reason a long-lived key existed at all.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Agglomerative clustering: linkages and the dendrogram
md: The scikit-learn guide warns that agglomerative clustering has a "rich get richer" behaviour that leads to uneven cluster sizes, with single linkage the worst and Ward the most regular. Its linkage comparison example adds that single linkage "performs poorly in the presence of noise" while Ward is "the most effective method for noisy data".

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Inside a vectorized pipeline: primitives and selection vectors
md: A selection vector is not a filtered copy. Downstream primitives read the original vectors at the listed positions. That avoids copying, but the reads are now indirect and sparse, which matters for SIMD (next lesson).

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Vectorization and why -O2 and -O3 differ on loops
md: Vectorization processes several elements per instruction, but only when the compiler can prove it is safe: known trip counts and non-overlapping pointers help. -O2 in GCC vectorizes only the easy cases (no runtime checks, and before GCC 15 no epilogue); -O3 also takes loops that need runtime alias checks.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Measure it: benchmarking builds and an end-to-end tuning run
md: Misconception: "fewer instructions or higher IPC means faster." Here -O0 had the best IPC and the worst time, and -O2 versus -O3 showed a 60 ms median gap with identical instructions. Time is the result; instructions, IPC and cache misses are clues that explain it.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong
md: An atomic load followed by an atomic store is **not** an atomic read-modify-write. The fix here is `num.fetch_add(1, AcqRel)`, which makes L and S one indivisible step. Atomics remove data races; they do not remove race conditions in your logic.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: Why one big ODE step from noise collapses to the mean
md: A diffusion model knows the *local* direction at each point. One-step generation needs the *global* answer: where does the whole trajectory end? A consistency model learns that endpoint directly.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Why hash mod N reshuffles almost every key
md: The goal of consistent hashing: when the set of servers changes, move only the keys that must move, which is about $K/N$ keys for $K$ keys and $N$ servers, and never shuffle keys between servers that did not change.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Decay functions turn distance and recency into smooth scores
md: A missing field scores **1**, the best possible decay value, in both Elasticsearch and OpenSearch. Profiles with no location beat everyone who lives a few kilometers away. Decide explicitly: require the field with an `exists` filter (it keeps only documents that have a value in that field), index a default value, or accept the behavior on purpose.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: CP-SAT in practice: lazy clauses, models and statuses
md: A solver turns a declarative model into search plus propagation plus learning. Your job is the model: tight domains, global constraints instead of many small ones, integer scaling, and a time limit with a status check.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: A hardened pod spec, line by line
md: Misconception: "runAsNonRoot is enough". It stops UID 0, but a non-root process with `allowPrivilegeEscalation` left at its default of true can still become root through a setuid binary in the image. Set both, and drop capabilities.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pod Security Admission and policy engines
md: Label every namespace with a Pod Security level: Restricted for applications, Baseline at minimum, Privileged only for reviewed system namespaces. Add a policy engine for rules PSA cannot express, and treat its webhook as critical infrastructure.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime detection with Falco and the Kubernetes audit log
md: Use both views: the audit log for who changed what through the API, and a syscall-level sensor such as Falco for what processes actually do. Each covers the other's blind spot.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: A five-turn session: diffs, state and generated queries
md: Strict mode guarantees the diff is **schema-valid**, not that it is **right**. A perfectly typed `{"remove": []}` for *drop the salary limit* is still a wrong state. Schema enforcement removes parsing failures; only evaluation (lesson 6) catches meaning failures.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Plausible is not faithful: the biasing-feature test
md: Faithfulness is a causal claim about what drove the answer. You test it by intervening, not by reading. A biasing feature that flips answers without ever being mentioned proves the CoT omitted a real cause.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: A worked pipeline: four chunks, and the copy-bound crossover
md: Overlap hides the smaller stages behind the largest one; it never removes the largest one. Your speedup ceiling is $(\sum_s t_s) / (\max_s t_s)$, reached as $n$ grows, and in the steady state the pipeline runs at the rate of its slowest stage. Before adding streams, work out which stage that is. If it is already the kernel, overlap buys you the copies and nothing more.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation
md: Reranker latency is about k divided by throughput. You control it with three knobs: how many candidates you rerank, how large the model is, and how many pairs you can run in parallel. Each trades against accuracy or cost.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: MACs and HMAC: integrity with a shared key
md: Never build a MAC from hash(key + message), and never compare secrets with ==. Use HMAC (or an AEAD, which includes a MAC) and hmac.compare_digest.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Bleichenbacher and ROBOT: retiring RSA key exchange
md: "We patched the oracle" is weaker than "we removed RSA key exchange". ROBOT found new oracles in implementations that already had Bleichenbacher countermeasures, because a single timing or TCP behaviour difference is enough.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Downgrade and protocol confusion: one key, one purpose
md: Security is set by the weakest place a key is accepted and the weakest option a negotiation allows. Give each key one job in one protocol, put the job's name inside everything it signs, and remove options rather than defending them.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization
md: A Hopper CUTLASS mainloop is a ring of shared memory stages: a producer warp keeps TMA loads ahead, consumer warpgroups run wgmma on full stages, and full and empty barriers pass ownership of each stage back and forth.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
md: Treat CXL memory as a far NUMA node: same instructions, same caching, about 70 to 100 ns more per miss for a nearby device, bandwidth comparable to a DDR channel per x8 link. Whether it is a win depends on how many misses you send there.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Van Buren (2021): gates up or down, not good or bad motives
md: After Van Buren: 'without authorization' asks whether you may enter the system at all; 'exceeds authorized access' asks whether you entered an area your access does not extend to. Motive is not the test. DOJ policy adds: decline good-faith research, and do not charge contract-only theories.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Copyright and trade secrets: DMCA section 1201 and Megamos Crypto
md: The exemption itself says it is "not a safe harbor from, or defense to" other laws, naming the CFAA. Circumventing a TPM on someone else's server can be legal under 1201 and still be unauthorised access. And the exemption covers the act of circumvention, not distributing circumvention tools.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Professional ethics: ISC2, ACM, the Menlo Report and the UMN patches
md: "The IRB said it was not human research" and "no bug was merged" did not end the matter. Ethics review is a floor, like law. If your study manipulates people's behaviour, they are participants, whatever the form says.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The 3-step pipeline and what it did to The Pile
md: Domain weights are not a zero-sum allocation of quality. Because very easy and very noisy domains need few samples, and domains transfer to each other, a better mixture can lower loss on **every** domain at once, including the ones it shrinks.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Curation inside a domain: quality filters from phi-1 to FineWeb-Edu
md: Think in two levels. **Within** a domain, clean and filter documents (lesson 9's rules and deduplication, then a classifier). **Across** domains, choose weights with a method like DoReMi or a fitted mixing model. Then rerun the mixing step, because filtering changes each domain's size and difficulty.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Seeing security from the data's side: copies, states and stages
md: Start every data security question from the data: what is it, where are *all* its copies (including tickets, exports and backups), who can read each one, how can it leave, and when will each copy be destroyed.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Database security I: accounts, grants, views and the revoke trap
md: Separate owner, application, analyst and admin roles; grant explicit columns or views rather than whole tables; never rely on revoking one column from a table-level grant; and keep grants in version control so drift is visible.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Two orderings, two answers: float addition is not associative
md: Floating-point addition is commutative but not associative. Reordering a sum is not a refactor, it is a different computation. Every other idea in this course follows from that sentence.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: DevSecOps: security checks on the path from commit to cloud
md: The pipeline is a privileged identity. Its definition files, its runners, its credentials and its state files deserve the same protection as production, because each one is a path into production.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why generate text in any order other than left to right?
md: A diffusion language model keeps the Transformer and the maximum-likelihood goal of a GPT. It changes two things: attention is bidirectional, and generation fills in many masked positions per step in any order instead of one token at the end.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Making diffusion LMs useful: AR initialization, RL and remasking
md: The mechanism of a diffusion LM is unchanged by all three ideas. AR initialization reuses weights through the shift operation, RL and DPO replace the exact log-probability with cheap or variance-reduced estimates of the bound, and ReMDM changes only the sampler so that more steps can fix mistakes.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins
md: Disaggregation adds failure modes. DistServe notes a fault in one decode instance that serves several prefill instances can spread, and FCFS prefill can create a convoy effect where long prompts block short ones. Mooncake must sometimes reject a request after its prefill if no decode slot is left, wasting that prefill.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Shortcuts, Jump Lists, ShellBags and the Recycle Bin
md: These artefacts show that a *user account* interacted with a file, a folder or a drive. They are strongest together and with the drive in hand.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking
md: Beam width W trades round trips for wasted reads; search list L trades reads for recall. Tune L for the recall target first, then pick the smallest W that meets the latency target, watching total reads against the SSD's IOPS budget.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
md: Turning a pair into one desirable and one undesirable example, as the paper does to compare against DPO, is described by its authors as a naive assumption: a chosen answer is only better than its sibling, not necessarily good.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Not every mismatch is a bug in the new store. If the new store is fed asynchronously, from a queue or a CDC stream, it is eventually consistent with the old one: a read right after a write can compare a fresh control with a candidate that is milliseconds behind. Measure that lag, and only `ignore` such cases after confirming they converge.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
md: Common misconception: "eBPF is safe, so tracing can't hurt production." The verifier guarantees the kernel won't crash or hang, but it does not bound *how often* your program runs. A kprobe on a function called millions of times per second can still cost a large fraction of every CPU.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Why appliances are hard to defend: patches, logs and trust
md: Treat an appliance as a server you cannot see into. Get its logs out as they are written, limit the secrets it holds, and plan in advance for the day you must rebuild it.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Detecting a compromised appliance from the outside
md: When you cannot see inside a device, watch its edges: every connection it starts, every session that changes address, every account that uses it, and every configuration change. Those records live on other systems the intruder does not control.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: L1: putting the token budget in the prompt
md: Length control needs an online reward that sees the generated length. The prompt carries the budget; the RL reward is what teaches the model to honor it.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Process injection as telemetry: Sysmon events 8, 10 and 25
md: Misconception: "a GrantedAccess of 0x1FFFFF on LSASS is always an attack." Security products, backup agents and admin tools often request all access. Context decides: which signed program, how often, from which path, and with which call trace. Baseline the normal requesters on your hosts, then alert on the rest.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
md: NILM is an inverse problem: one observed sum, many hidden parts. Every algorithm you will meet differs only in what extra knowledge it uses to choose among the many decompositions that add up to the same total.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Blocking: compare only pairs that could match
md: A pair that blocking drops is classified as a non-match without ever being looked at. No scoring model can recover it. Use several strict rules joined by OR (Splink's advice: a longer list of strict rules beats a short list of loose ones), so a typo in one field is caught by a rule on another.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM
md: A service principal can hold an Entra admin role, and Microsoft names those that do as control plane assets. An app with Global Administrator, or with permission to assign roles, is a Global Administrator that has no MFA prompt to bypass. Review apps in role assignments with the same care as people.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Entra tokens: lifetimes, refresh tokens and revocation
md: Misconception: resetting a compromised user's password ends the attacker's access immediately. It revokes only refresh tokens obtained with the password (revoke sessions for the rest), and an access token already issued keeps working until it expires (up to 90 minutes) at any service that does not support CAE, and app sessions with their own cookies (the federation course's offboarding gap) are untouched.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Conditional Access in Entra: baselines and the gaps attackers use
md: Misconception: 'We have Conditional Access requiring MFA, so password spraying is solved.' Only for accounts and flows the policies cover. Excluded service accounts, legacy protocols if not blocked, and service principals with secrets all sit outside it, and attackers spray exactly those.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: A hardening baseline, an incident runbook, and where to practise
md: Baseline: few cloud-only admins on passkeys through PIM, restricted consent and reviewed apps, legacy auth and device code blocked, device-bound tokens where possible, hybrid bridges as Tier 0, and every log exported. Runbook: contain identities, hunt persistence in apps, devices and federation, scope data, evict at the root.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
md: Misconception: "we never trained on the test queries, so the number is clean." Choosing among variants by their test score is training with a very small model: one decision per comparison. A hundred prompt tweaks checked against the same 50 queries is a hundred-way fit.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: From bug to control: why exploit mitigations exist
md: A mitigation does not remove the bug. It removes one *route* from the bug to control. Patch the bug, prefer memory-safe languages for new code, and treat mitigations as the layer that protects you from the bugs you have not found yet.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
md: The unit of sharing between cores is the cache line, not the variable. Two variables in one line are shared as far as the hardware is concerned, whatever the source code says.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
md: With $E = 1$, full batches and full participation, FedAvg is exactly full-batch gradient descent on the pooled objective. Everything interesting about federated optimization, good and bad, comes from doing more than one local step.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Choosing gamma, falling back to pre-filter, and real results
md: ACORN is not free accuracy. The paper gives no connectivity guarantee for arbitrary data (neither does HNSW); connectivity is shown empirically. Very selective or strongly clustered predicates still need the pre-filter fallback, and ACORN-$\gamma$'s build is far slower than HNSW (SIFT1M 148.9 s vs 11.3 s, LAION-25M 38,007.5 s vs 1,147.2 s).

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Counting the work: FLOPs, bytes, and the exponential unit
md: Misconception: "attention is two GEMMs, so it runs at GEMM speed." The softmax between them is cheap in FLOPs but runs on units hundreds of times slower than the tensor cores. FP8 makes it worse: matmul throughput doubles while exponential throughput stays the same.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Crossing lines and why the learned paths curve
md: Straight training targets do not mean straight sampling paths. Each conditional path is a line, but the marginal flow, which is what the network learns and what sampling follows, curves wherever many lines cross.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Refinement: proving a detailed design implements an abstract one
md: Refinement says nothing about the steps the mapping hides. If the mapping ignores a variable that matters (say, durable state on disk), a wrong design can still refine the spec. Review the mapping as carefully as the spec.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: "FP8 training" does not mean every tensor is FP8. In the FP8 paper, DeepSeek-V3 and the NVFP4 report alike, only the *inputs* to GEMMs are FP8. GEMM outputs come out in BF16 or FP32, and normalizations, softmax, the master weights and optimizer state stay in higher precision. Lesson 4 shows what that means for memory and speed, and the recipes that push FP8 into communication and optimizer state too.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a fake quantizer for E4M3, MXFP4 and NVFP4
md: A fake quantizer reproduces a format's numerics, not its speed: what each value becomes after casting and scaling. Real hardware adds its own accumulation precision and order, so validate surprising results on the target GPU, but use the fake quantizer to test a recipe on your own tensors first.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
md: On macOS, Apple's Xcode clang ships without libFuzzer (the Atheris documentation says the same), and Homebrew's clang needs the SDK path (`-isysroot $(xcrun --show-sdk-path)`) to find system headers. On Linux, distribution clang packages include it.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
md: The Broadcom case was found by reverse engineering and code review, not fuzzing, and its lesson for fuzzers is about reach: the dangerous code ran only for specific frame types in specific connection states. A stateless fuzzer of single frames would rarely get there.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Why exact matching fails and what an edit distance counts
md: A distance counts edits (lower is closer). A similarity is a normalized score (higher is closer). The same raw distance means very different things for short and long strings, so either normalize or make the allowed number of edits depend on length.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
md: Geometric hashing moves the expensive work offline: every model is stored under every basis. At query time one correct scene basis is enough, and it never needs to know in advance which model point it corresponds to.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Geohash: interleave the bits, name the cell
md: A shared geohash prefix guarantees closeness: both points are inside the same cell. The reverse is false: two points can be meters apart and share no prefix, because they straddle a cell boundary. Every correct proximity search must look at neighboring cells, not just one prefix.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
md: A caching allocator turns slow, synchronizing driver calls into fast CPU-side bookkeeping. The price is that freed memory is *kept*, so reserved memory, not allocated memory, is what other processes on the GPU see.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Fixed-size suballocation for the KV cache, and diagnosing OOMs
md: All of these allocators are the same pattern at different layers: grab big memory rarely, carve it with your own rules, and choose block sizes that match the workload. Equal sizes kill external fragmentation; growable virtual ranges kill slivers; stream order makes reuse cheap.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
md: These measurements come from older GPUs (Fermi and Kepler in the post, Volta in the guide). Absolute numbers on a current GPU will differ, and larger caches can hide some waste. The sector and bank rules they illustrate are the ones the current CUDA guides still document.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
md: Rank by gap times time share, with an attainable target instead of 100 percent. The biggest gap and the biggest win are usually different kernels, and a gap on a kernel with a small time share is never worth a rewrite.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
md: GraphRAG is not a better retriever for every question. For a specific fact ("Who supplies Rover X2 motors?") plain vector RAG already finds c2, and the paper itself shows vector RAG gives the most *direct* answers. GraphRAG's measured gains are on broad sensemaking questions, the ones that need an understanding of the whole corpus.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
md: Graph RAG variants differ in where they spend LLM calls: GraphRAG spends heavily at indexing (extraction, summaries, reports) and on map calls per global query; FastGraphRAG cuts extraction; LightRAG drops communities; HippoRAG drops summaries and lets PPR do the multi-hop work.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: RLOO, GSPO, off-policy drift, and what RLVR teaches
md: Before trusting an RLVR gain: test on several model families (a Qwen-only result may be amplified priors), compare against random and format-only rewards, and compare against distilling a stronger model (lesson 6).

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf stat: counting, multiplexing and scaled estimates
md: A percentage in parentheses after a `perf stat` line, like `(74.98%)`, means that event ran only that fraction of the time and was scaled. Treat such numbers as estimates, and be most suspicious when the workload has phases.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Trusted hardware: TPMs, measured boot and secure enclaves
md: An enclave or TEE protects against software that cannot reach its memory. It does not remove side channels: if enclave code runs on the same core as the attacker, its cache footprint, branch history and timing are as observable as any other program's. Enclave code must still be constant-time.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
md: Do not over-learn the Redis story as "THP copy-on-write always copies 2 MiB". In current `mm/huge_memory.c`, a write to a shared anonymous THP splits the mapping and copies one 4 KiB page. What remains true is that fork-heavy writers churn their huge mappings, and the projects' own guidance (Redis: disable THP; PostgreSQL: THP currently discouraged, explicit huge_pages recommended) is what to follow.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short
md: Design rule of thumb from published ablations: keep roughly 8% to 12% of layers as global attention, spread them evenly, start with an SSM layer, and expect long-context KV savings close to (attention layers in the Transformer you replace) / (attention layers you keep), at equal KV heads: 32 / 4 = 8x for Nemotron-H-8B vs Nemotron-T-8B, not 52 / 4 = 13x.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Latency, cost, and when HyDE hurts
md: Use HyDE where its strength is real: no labels, a weak or unsupervised encoder, domain or format shift, and a latency budget of seconds. Keep the query in the average, cap passage length, sample in parallel, and route by query type. The paper itself suggests serving HyDE early, then shifting traffic to a supervised retriever as logs grow, keeping HyDE for rare and emerging queries.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: DNP3, S7comm and OPC UA: from no security to secure by design
md: Ask two questions of any industrial protocol: does the receiver verify who sent this command, and can it tell if the command was changed or replayed? For classic Modbus and plain DNP3 the answer is no, so the network around them must do that job.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Incident response in OT: safety first, then manual
md: In OT incident response, first make the process safe (using instruments you trust), then keep it running by hand if needed, and only then contain, investigate and restore from offline backups.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Case: ruby-saml CVE-2024-45409 and the GitLab SAML bypass (2024)
md: MFA at the IdP protects the IdP's login. It does nothing for an SP whose verification code can be fooled, because the attacker skips the IdP entirely. Patch SAML libraries as fast as you patch internet-facing servers, and correlate SP logins with IdP sign-ins.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Case: Okta's support system and the stolen HAR files (2023)
md: Session tokens are credentials, wherever they are written down: HAR files, logs, screenshots, crash dumps. Shorten their lives, bind them to the network or device they were issued to, and treat any system that stores them (a support desk included) as part of your identity perimeter.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Privileged access: why admin rights differ, and the Snowden case
md: Administrators are trusted to touch everything, so their misuse looks like their job. Detection only works if privileged activity is logged somewhere the administrator cannot edit, and reviewed by someone else (AC-5 and AC-6(9), log the use of privileged functions).

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Rejecting bad matches, warping, and direct ECC alignment
md: Those border zeros look like a dark region in the warped image, and subtracting it from the reference flags a band of fake change along the edges. Warp an all-ones image with the same H to get a validity mask, and ignore pixels outside it.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Preparation: plan, people, contacts, retainers and logs
md: A plan that has never been exercised is a guess. The HSE review recommends testing plans against a catastrophic ransomware scenario in which all IT, all security tools and all usual communication channels are unavailable for weeks.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Building a timeline: super timelines, plaso and a worked merge
md: Never mix time zones silently. Convert everything to UTC at ingestion and keep the original value and its assumed zone, so that a later correction (a server set to the wrong zone, a drifting clock) can be applied and explained.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Heartland and TalkTalk: SQL injection as the way in
md: Both breaches started with a well-known bug class in a web page, and both turned into something much larger: lateral movement into a payment network in one case, and a forgotten set of acquired pages exposing a customer database in the other. You cannot fix pages you do not know you run, so asset inventory is a defence against injection too.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Submitting, waiting and how the kernel runs a request
md: A classic bug: `char buf[4096];` on the stack of a function that preps a read, submits, and returns. The kernel later writes 4096 bytes into a stack frame that now belongs to someone else. Buffers belong to the kernel from submission until the matching CQE.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Gadgets: from a polluted prototype to code execution (Kibana)
md: Do not read the hardening as "pollution is solved". It closes gadgets inside Node.js's own child_process code only. Your framework, template engine, HTTP client and your own options objects are full of optional properties, and every one is a possible gadget. The fix is still to stop pollution at the source.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Electron: when XSS in a desktop app becomes code execution
md: In Electron, every XSS is a candidate for code execution on the user's machine. The defaults (nodeIntegration off, contextIsolation on, sandbox on) are what keep XSS confined to the page; an app that turns any of them off, or runs an old Electron, has removed a wall. Lesson 16 covers the remaining walls you build yourself.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Histories: invoke, ok, fail, and the indeterminate info
md: Misconception: "a timeout means the request failed." A timeout means *you stopped waiting*. Writes, compare-and-sets and transaction commits that time out must be recorded as `:info` unless the error proves nothing was applied (for example, the request was rejected before it was sent).

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
md: The most common autotuning self-deception is a "win" smaller than the confidence interval of the comparison. Report the interval, not just the ratio, and treat an interval that straddles 1.0 as "no difference found", not as a win.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
md: Bypass trades generality for cycles. It wins when per-operation overhead is the bottleneck and you can dedicate cores and devices; it loses when you need the kernel's protocols, tools, filesystems, isolation or power savings.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Temperature: amplifying the small probabilities
md: Temperature does not change the argmax, the class with the highest score. Running the deployed student at T greater than 1 does not change its top-1 predictions at all; it only makes its probabilities less confident. Temperature is a training-time device for distillation (and a separate sampling knob for generative models).

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: An LLM distillation pipeline: logits, tokenizers, traces, compute
md: Before writing an LLM distillation loss: confirm a teacher exists or will be reused; use logits when you can, text (Seq-KD, traces) when you cannot; store top-k with a tail bucket or mix in data loss; switch to a sorted-probability loss across tokenizers; and consider starting the student from a pruned teacher.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)
md: Bits per number are not the whole cost. Group metadata adds bits (about 1 per number for FP16 scale and zero per 32), and the full-precision residual matters for short sequences.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go
md: Each tier down is roughly 10x bigger and slower. Offloading turns a prefix-cache miss into a load from a lower tier, which pays off only if the load is faster than recomputing.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Why wall clocks cannot order events across machines
md: A smaller wall-clock reading does not mean an event happened before another, and an event that did happen first can carry a larger wall-clock reading, as the last-write-wins example shows. Treat wall time as a hint, never as proof of order.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Storage: why token vectors are heavy and how ColBERTv2 shrinks them
md: Compression is lossy per vector, and the 1-bit setting does cost measurable quality. Treat 2-bit as the safe default and verify 1-bit on your own evaluation set before shipping it.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Teaching a model to think without words: the curriculum
md: The objective never asks a thought to compress the step it replaced. Thoughts are trained only by how much they help predict the remaining steps and the answer, so they are free to become something other than a paraphrase of the text.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index
md: Do not read stage-0 output as a position. In the example it predicts 3.75 for key 1, which is at position 0. Stage 0 is graded only on whether it routes keys to leaves that can fit them, not on its own accuracy.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: SPLADE v2, SPLADE++ and running it in production
md: Do not read the tokens as an explanation. Elastic's docs warn that expansion terms are learned associations, not synonyms, and that low-weight tokens carry information jointly, much like dimensions of a dense vector. A surprising token in a result is not by itself a bug.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
md: Linear attention is not a cheap approximation of softmax attention that converges to it. The exponential kernel has an infinite-dimensional feature map (Katharopoulos et al.), so any finite state is a different, weaker model. That gap is what the rest of this course is about.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Where things live: the Linux filesystem from a defender's view
md: A detail worth remembering for later: if a program's file is deleted while it is still running, `/proc/<pid>/exe` shows the original path with ` (deleted)` appended (`proc_pid_exe(5)`). Legitimate software rarely does this; a process running from a deleted file in `/tmp` is a classic sign of an intruder cleaning up after starting a tool.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Packages and updates, and the xz-utils backdoor
md: Patching closes most known holes, so do it promptly and automatically where you can, and reboot when the kernel or core libraries change. Package signatures protect the path from repository to you; they cannot vouch for the people upstream.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: One host is a checklist, a fleet is a control loop
md: A baseline you apply once decays. Write it down, apply it with an idempotent tool on a schedule, scan for drift, and stream telemetry off every host. The rest of this course fills in each box of that loop.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: The Linux audit system: how a system call becomes a record
md: Audit records come from the kernel, not the program, and one event is several records sharing TIME:SERIAL. auid (the login uid) is set once at login and survives su and sudo, which is what lets you attribute root actions to a person.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tetragon: filtering and enforcing inside the kernel
md: Tetragon filters in the kernel and can act there. Hook LSM functions such as security_file_permission rather than raw system call arguments, start in observe mode, and pair Sigkill with Override when the operation itself must not happen.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Immutable OS images: rebuild instead of repair
md: Immutable does not mean uncompromisable. A remote bug still gives an attacker code execution in memory until the next reboot, and writable areas still persist. Keep runtime telemetry; immutability shrinks persistence, not intrusion.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Why open-ended output is hard to score
md: An evaluator is a measuring instrument. Before trusting any number it produces, check how often it agrees with careful human judgment on your task, at the level (single output or whole system) at which you will use it.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: policies, strengths and grounding
md: Read the coverage notes, not just the feature list. Per the AWS docs, sensitive information filters do not mask PII the model writes into tool call arguments, and grounding checks on a streamed response (one sent to the user piece by piece as it is generated) may mark it irrelevant only after it has been streamed. A guardrail protects only the channels it actually inspects.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
md: Preemption is not free throughput. The optimistic policy's extra batch size is partly spent redoing prefills, and a preempted request's latency can jump by a full prefill plus queueing. Frequent preemption is a sign the pool is too small for the configured concurrency.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Validation, retries and the pitfalls of strict formats
md: Treat structured output as a contract with three checks: did it finish (stop reason), does it fit (schema, often enforced by the decoder), and is it right (your validators and evals, test sets of inputs with known good answers). Leave the model an honest way out, put reasoning before answers, and measure quality with and without the constraint.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Anatomy of one rerank call: tokens in, tokens out, two phases
md: Misconception: "output is only 60 tokens, so it is negligible." For billing it is small. For latency it is not, because prefill reads thousands of tokens in parallel while decode produces tokens one step at a time.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Why use an LLM as the last-stage reranker
md: An LLM reranker is a prompt plus an aggregation rule. Pointwise, pairwise and listwise differ in what one call sees (1, 2 or a window of passages) and therefore in how many calls a ranking needs and how hard each call is.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Why corners make good features: the Harris response
md: Harris is invariant to rotation (eigenvalues do not change when the image rotates) but **not to scale**. Zoom in on a corner enough and, inside a fixed 3x3 window, it looks like an edge. Lesson 2 fixes this.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
md: Lock-free means a stalled thread can never stop the others: some operation always completes. It does not promise that any particular thread finishes, and it does not promise speed under contention.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Why one regular expression per format does not scale
md: A common dodge: "I will write regexes only for the formats I care about and drop the rest." You cannot know in advance which format you will care about during the next incident, and the lines you dropped are exactly the rare error templates. Dropping them also silently biases every count you compute afterwards.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: What to log, source by source
md: Never write secrets into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet lists data to exclude or mask: passwords, access tokens, session identifiers (hash them if you need to follow a session), encryption keys, connection strings and sensitive personal data. Logs are copied widely, so anything in them leaks widely.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Tuning and allowlisting without blinding yourself
md: Every allowlist entry is a promise that this pattern will never be malicious. Prefer fields the attacker cannot set (exact path in a protected folder, code-signing publisher, asset group from your inventory) over fields they can (process name, command-line text, user agent, file name).

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
md: YaRN = per-pair ramp on rotations $r = L/\lambda$ (keep fast pairs, fully interpolate slow ones, blend between) plus a logit temperature $\sqrt{1/t} = 0.1\ln s + 1$, all baked into the precomputed cos and sin tables.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Universal Transformers: recurrence over depth with a halting rule
md: Dynamic halting is not free accuracy. It helped on bAbI and LAMBADA but slightly hurt translation, adds a ponder-cost hyperparameter, and makes different positions in a batch finish at different times.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: When looping helps, when it hurts, and the design space
md: Looping buys **depth** (multi-step reasoning, using context), not **capacity** (memorized facts). Judge a looped model on reasoning tasks at matched FLOPs, not only on perplexity at matched parameters.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short
md: Hu et al.'s footnote already warned that a small rank should not be expected to work for every task: if the target were a different language than pretraining, full fine-tuning (like LoRA with r equal to the model width) could win. Low intrinsic rank was measured on tasks that are close to what the model already knows.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
md: Low scores on forget benchmarks show suppressed outputs, not erased knowledge. Small fine-tunes, probes and even 4-bit quantization can bring "forgotten" knowledge back, because approximate unlearning moves the weights only slightly.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Disassemblers and decompilers: from bytes back to C
md: Reversing is a loop of hypotheses: name what you think a function does, check it against the assembly and against dynamic behaviour, and rename again. Stuxnet's analysts needed months and domain experts; your first samples will need hours. The method is the same.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Sharing intelligence and writing the analysis report
md: Write for the reader who must act. The executive summary is for the person deciding whether to isolate fifty machines; the indicators and rules are for the people who will do it. Separate observed facts from your assessments, and say how confident you are.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Tensor parallelism: column and row splits of the MLP and attention
md: Misconception: more TP is a free way to save memory. Per-GPU TP traffic stays near 8bsh per layer however large t gets, every GEMM gets t times smaller (lower GPU efficiency), and once t exceeds the GPUs in one server the all-reduces leave NVLink for the much slower network. Narayanan et al.'s Takeaway 1: use TP up to the server size (8 on DGX A100), then PP across servers.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Acquiring RAM: WinPmem, DumpIt, LiME, AVML and virtual machines
md: Every acquisition changes the system it copies: the tool's process, its driver or module, and the memory they allocate all land in the image. LiME's README even warns that its optional digest and compression features disturb more of the target's memory. Record the tool, version, command and time so the footprint can be told apart from the attacker's.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Timelines from memory: what carries a time, and merging it
md: Memory gives you the start times of what is running now and a few remnants of what ran before. Disk gives you the long history. The overlap, a process in memory whose start matches a Prefetch run and a 4688 event, is where a timeline becomes solid.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Why freed memory does not go back: pages, arenas, purging
md: Setting `dirty_decay_ms` to 0 is not a free fix. The manual says it purges dirty pages immediately when they are created, so every page that empties pays for a purge, and every later reuse pays a page fault. It lowers RSS that is merely waiting; it does nothing for pages pinned by live objects.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Why freeing a removed node is the hard part
md: A garbage collector does not make ABA impossible in every case. Michael points out that if a program moves the same live node back and forth between two lists, ABA can still occur even with perfect GC. What a GC (and the schemes in this course) guarantees is narrower: a node's address is not reused while someone can still reach it.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
md: Grace periods (EBR, RCU) make reads cheap but let one stalled reader block all reclamation. Hazard pointers bound garbage at N x R but charge every visited node. Pick by read pattern and by how much you trust threads to keep moving.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Use-after-free and double free: dangling pointers
md: Chromium reports that about 70 percent of its high-severity security bugs are memory safety problems, and that half of those are use-after-free. Lifetimes are the hardest promise to keep by hand in a large C++ program.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
md: Sample P identities x K images so every batch contains positives and look-alike negatives, then mine within the batch. Mining becomes a max and a min over a distance matrix you already have.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
md: Misconception: "disabling ASLR and pinning the CPU makes my benchmark correct". They reduce run-to-run noise, which narrows intervals. A narrow interval around a biased setup is a confidently wrong answer.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Moving a trillion parameters, and surviving dead engines
md: The Miles fault-tolerance page is marked **outdated**: it describes the pre-refactor stack, and new machinery is still being merged. Also note that P2P writes are bounded by `--p2p-transfer-timeout` (default 30 s) and a failed write fails the update; the docs state there is no automatic retry or fallback to broadcast.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
md: Reported speedups are relative to specific baselines on specific traces: B-LRU on six CDN traces, a tuned weighted fair scheduler on TPC-H mixes, a read-optimized B-tree on read-only integer keys. A different workload, or a stronger baseline, can shrink the gain to zero.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Content providers and shared files: from URI grants to Dirty Stream
md: A shared file arrives with two attacker-controlled things: its content and its name. Treat both as untrusted input. Choose your own name, and parse the content as hostile.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Low-rank joint compression: cache one latent, rebuild every head
md: MLA is not a compression applied to an already trained model's cache, like PCA (principal component analysis, which finds the few directions that capture most of the variation in a set of vectors) run on stored keys. The down- and up-projections are ordinary weights learned from scratch during pretraining. Converting an existing MHA or GQA model to MLA needs extra fine-tuning work (see lesson 7).

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
md: Unmerged does not mean easy. Requests in one batch use adapters with different ranks and different sequence lengths, so padding everything into one batched matmul wastes work. S-LoRA's variant that copies adapters into contiguous memory and uses padded batched matmul (S-LoRA-bmm) was much slower than the version with custom kernels, GPU functions written for exactly this mixed-rank job.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
md: RRF rewards agreement between phrasings. A relevant document that only one phrasing finds stays low, and a junk document that two phrasings share can outrank it. That is why the quality of the phrasings matters as much as their number.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Common misconception: an MTP model does not have to emit several tokens per step. Gloeckle et al. use only the next-token head for ordinary decoding. The other heads are optional, and lesson 7 shows how they can be reused to draft tokens for faster decoding.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why orthogonalize: steepest descent under the spectral norm
md: Pick the ruler, get the optimizer. Frobenius gives gradient descent, the largest-entry norm gives sign descent (Adam without moving averages), the spectral norm gives the orthogonalized update. For a hidden linear layer the spectral norm is the one that bounds how much its outputs move.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Choosing an optimizer: how much faster is it really?
md: Do not judge an optimizer by a single untuned comparison. The Muon post argues that the most common reason optimizers that claimed to beat AdamW never caught on is an undertuned AdamW baseline, and proposes competitive benchmarks (like the NanoGPT speedrun record, where anyone can revert to AdamW) as the standard of evidence.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: The muP rules, layer by layer
md: Every piece is needed. Keeping $1/\sqrt{d}$ attention, using plain `torch.optim.Adam` instead of `MuAdam`, or forgetting to scale `d_ffn` along with `d_model` silently breaks transfer while the model still trains. Lesson 7 shows how to catch this.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
md: A lock is two things at once: mutual exclusion (one atomic read-modify-write decides a single winner) and visibility (Acquire on lock, Release on unlock, so each unlock happens-before the next lock).

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
md: MVCC is not the same as no locking. Two transactions that update the *same* row still conflict: the second one waits for the first to commit or roll back. MVCC only stops readers and writers from blocking each other.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: catching dangerous structures
md: SSI = snapshot isolation plus non-blocking tracking of rw edges. It aborts a transaction in any dangerous structure, so every committed set is serializable; the application's job is to retry on 40001.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Why long context needs sparsity, and why bolt-on sparsity disappoints
md: Theoretical FLOP savings are not speedups. A sparse attention method is only fast if the GPU reads fewer bytes in contiguous chunks during every phase (training, prefill, decode), and it only keeps quality if the model is trained with the sparsity.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: pHash: hashing the low frequencies of a DCT
md: aHash compares pixels with the mean, dHash compares neighbors, pHash compares low-frequency DCT coefficients with their median. All three are **global**: they describe the whole frame at fixed positions, which is why resizing and tone changes are cheap to survive and crops, flips and rotations are not.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Where the attacker stands: on-path, off-path and on your LAN
md: Know the position before you pick the defence. Encryption (TLS) defeats on-path reading and rewriting of content. Unpredictable numbers (random ports, sequence numbers, IDs) defeat off-path guessing. Switch features such as MAC limiting, DHCP snooping and ARP inspection stop local attackers from becoming on-path.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Flooding DNS and HTTP/2: Dyn 2016 and Rapid Reset 2023
md: Application-layer floods win through asymmetry: a cheap action for the client (open and cancel a stream) that is expensive for the server. Defences measure behaviour per connection and close abusive connections outright, because per-request blocking leaves the cheap channel open. The pattern recurs: MadeYouReset (CVE-2025-8671, 2025) uses malformed control frames to make the server reset streams itself.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Zeek's protocol logs and pivoting with uid, fuid and Community ID
md: Two IDs carry most investigations: Zeek's uid joins logs about one connection, fuid joins logs about one file. Community ID extends the join to other tools. Learn to move between them quickly; it is most of the job.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Network forensics for incident response: a worked IcedID investigation
md: Capture and analyse only traffic you own or are authorised to monitor. Practice pcaps of real infections contain working malware and sometimes real personal data from the lab: open them on an isolated, non-Windows machine and never run extracted files.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Ports, sockets and NAT
md: NAT is not a firewall. It drops unsolicited inbound packets only as a side effect of having no table entry. Port-forwarding rules, devices that open forwards automatically, IPv6 (often no NAT at all) and connections started from inside all bypass that "protection". Use an actual firewall policy.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
md: malloc chooses addresses, the first write chooses the node. Initialize data in parallel with the same pinned threads and the same partitioning that will later use it.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Wear leveling, TRIM, hot and cold data, endurance
md: Lifetime and throughput both scale with 1/A. The levers to lower A are all about making victim blocks emptier: more spare, TRIM of dead data, writes that are large and sequential, and grouping data that will die at the same time.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
